examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}5-4\cos x&=7\\-4\cos x&=2\\\cos x&=-\frac12\end{aligned}$

The reference angle is $\frac\pi3$. Cosine is negative in quadrants 2 and 3.

$\begin{aligned}x&=\pi-\frac\pi3,\ \pi+\frac\pi3\\x&=\frac{2\pi}3,\ \frac{4\pi}3\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}4\sin(3x)+1&=3\\4\sin(3x)&=2\\\sin(3x)&=\frac12\end{aligned}$

Let $u=3x$. The transformed domain is $0\le u\le3\pi$.

The reference angle is $\frac\pi6$. Sine is positive in quadrants 1 and 2. Add $2\pi$ to the first two angles to find the remaining angles in the domain.

$u=\frac\pi6,\ \frac{5\pi}6,\ \frac{13\pi}6,\ \frac{17\pi}6$.

$\begin{aligned}x&=\frac u3\\x&=\frac\pi{18},\ \frac{5\pi}{18},\ \frac{13\pi}{18},\ \frac{17\pi}{18}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}2\tan(3x)+2&=0\\2\tan(3x)&=-2\\\tan(3x)&=-1\end{aligned}$

Let $u=3x$, so $0\le u\le3\pi$.

The reference angle is $\frac\pi4$. Tangent is negative in quadrants 2 and 4 and repeats every $\pi$.

$u=\frac{3\pi}4,\ \frac{7\pi}4,\ \frac{11\pi}4$.

$\begin{aligned}x&=\frac u3\\x&=\frac\pi4,\ \frac{7\pi}{12},\ \frac{11\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}2\sin\left(2x+\frac\pi3\right)&=1\\\sin\left(2x+\frac\pi3\right)&=\frac12\end{aligned}$

Let $u=2x+\frac\pi3$. At $x=0$, $u=\frac\pi3$; at $x=2\pi$, $u=\frac{13\pi}3$.

The transformed domain is $\frac\pi3\le u\le\frac{13\pi}3$.

Sine equals $\frac12$ at angles $\frac\pi6$ and $\frac{5\pi}6$, repeated every $2\pi$. Keeping only angles in the transformed domain gives

$u=\frac{5\pi}6,\ \frac{13\pi}6,\ \frac{17\pi}6,\ \frac{25\pi}6$.

$\begin{aligned}x&=\frac12\left(u-\frac\pi3\right)\\x&=\frac\pi4,\ \frac{11\pi}{12},\ \frac{5\pi}4,\ \frac{23\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}4\cos(2x)-2&=0\\4\cos(2x)&=2\\\cos(2x)&=\frac12\end{aligned}$

Let $u=2x$, so $-2\pi\le u\le2\pi$.

In $0\le u\le2\pi$, the solutions are $u=\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}3$. Subtract $2\pi$ from each to obtain the solutions in the negative half of the domain.

$u=-\frac{5\pi}3,\ -\frac\pi3,\ \frac\pi3,\ \frac{5\pi}3$.

$\begin{aligned}x&=\frac u2\\x&=-\frac{5\pi}6,\ -\frac\pi6,\ \frac\pi6,\ \frac{5\pi}6\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}4\sin\left(\frac x2\right)+1&=-1\\4\sin\left(\frac x2\right)&=-2\\\sin\left(\frac x2\right)&=-\frac12\end{aligned}$

Let $u=\frac x2$, so $0\le u\le2\pi$.

The reference angle is $\frac\pi6$. Sine is negative in quadrants 3 and 4.

$u=\frac{7\pi}6,\ \frac{11\pi}6$.

$\begin{aligned}x&=2u\\x&=\frac{7\pi}3,\ \frac{11\pi}3\end{aligned}$

examples.derivation: Rearranging gives cos x = -1/2. In [0,2π], the quadrant 2 and 3 angles give x = 2π/3, 4π/3.
Rearranging gives sin(3x) = 1/2. With u = 3x in [0,3π], u = π/6, 5π/6, 13π/6, 17π/6. Dividing by 3 gives x = π/18, 5π/18, 13π/18, 17π/18.
Rearranging gives tan(3x) = -1. With u = 3x in [0,3π], the π-periodic solutions are u = 3π/4, 7π/4, 11π/4. Hence x = π/4, 7π/12, 11π/12.
Let u = 2x + π/3, giving π/3 ≤ u ≤ 13π/3. For sin u = 1/2, the permitted angles are 5π/6, 13π/6, 17π/6, 25π/6. Applying x = (u - π/3)/2 gives π/4, 11π/12, 5π/4, 23π/12.
Rearranging gives cos(2x) = 1/2. With u = 2x in [-2π,2π], periodicity gives u = -5π/3, -π/3, π/3, 5π/3. Hence x = -5π/6, -π/6, π/6, 5π/6.
Rearranging gives sin(x/2) = -1/2. With u = x/2 in [0,2π], u = 7π/6, 11π/6. Multiplying by 2 gives x = 7π/3, 11π/3.
The isolated ratio is sin(2x) = -3/2, outside [-1,1], so there are no solutions. The plotted curve has range [2,6]; the red dashed line y = 1 lies below it throughout the domain.
Rearranging gives cos(2x) = 1. With u = 2x in [0,4π], u = 0, 2π, 4π, giving x = 0, π, 2π. The plotted curve has maxima y = 1 at precisely the three marked points.
